extracted.intended_audience: patent lawyers, judges, and law students; parties (assignors/assignees/vendees) involved in patent sales and assignments
extracted.subtask_description: Rules and standards governing rights, defenses, and remedies of assignors and assignees (venders/vendees) in sales or assignments of patent rights, including fraud, warranty, title defects, invalidity, and equitable relief. Focuses on when money may be recovered, when assignments may be rescinded, and what defenses are available.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rescission for fraud by vendor / mutual restoration
rubrics_metrics.description: A vendee induced by false representations may rescind the sale; the contract becomes void from its beginning and mutual restoration of all its results must follow.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A bill in equity to set aside the assignment must allege that no benefits have been received since discovery of the fraud and must offer to return those previously accrued. When the patented invention is entirely worthless and the assignee was induced by fraudulent representations as to value, the price may be recovered in a suit at law without prior rescission or offer to return the patent. But where parties were of equal knowledge or purchase money paid after full acquaintance with the facts, no action to recover will lie. If vendee exercises ownership after discovery of fraud, it will affirm the sale.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effect of equal knowledge or acquiescence
rubrics_metrics.description: If both vendor and vendee have equal knowledge (or equal fault) regarding the patent, equity will not relieve the vendee; the vendee who acquiesces and takes benefits cannot avoid the sale.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where parties were of equal knowledge or in equal fault, or where purchase money has been paid after full acquaintance with facts, no action to recover will lie. A vendee who exercises ownership over the patent after discovering fraud affirms the sale (see cases cited).

rubrics_metrics.name: Implied warranty of title in assignment
rubrics_metrics.description: An assignment of a patent raises an implied warranty of title, but not of the validity of the patent nor of the practical value of the patented invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Action for breach of warranty lies only where the title proves defective, unless the instrument contains express covenants warranting validity. Express covenants may relate directly to the patent or by implication warrant its validity and create rights vindicable by action at law for damages. Where assignor and assignee are both in equal ignorance concerning patentability, no implied warranty of validity arises.

rubrics_metrics.name: Vendee's burden to show disturbance or lack of right to convey
rubrics_metrics.description: A vendee suing on implied warranty must show that he has been disturbed in the enjoyment of the right, or that the vendor had no right which he could convey.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To recover on implied warranty the vendee must demonstrate disturbance in enjoyment of the patent right or that the vendor had no right to convey it (see Stevens v. Head and related notes).

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope of territorial exclusive-right warranty
rubrics_metrics.description: A warranty of exclusive right within a given territory extends only to the specific inventions conveyed to the vendee.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The covenant is not broader than the specific inventions assigned within the territory; territorial limits and specifics control extent of warranty (see Kingman v. Martin).

rubrics_metrics.name: Remedy when assignee refuses to accept conveyance
rubrics_metrics.description: If an assignee refuses to accept the conveyance when duly tendered, the assignor's remedy is generally a suit at law for damages; specific performance in equity is only available in special cases.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Equity will compel execution only when obligations are such that justice cannot be done at law—for example when consideration is conveyance of real property or surrender of essential rights. In such peculiar circumstances, specific performance may be ordered to require transfer or release of stipulated property or claim.

rubrics_metrics.name: Remedy for non-fulfilment of conditions in assignment
rubrics_metrics.description: For failure to perform conditions imposed by the assignment, the assignor may obtain damages at law; if conditions are essential to the assignee's title or to enjoyment of reserved rights, failure may forfeit the assignee's interest and equity may decree reconveyance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Conditions which are not expressly or impliedly promised to be performed but that operate as forfeitures cannot themselves be enforced in equity nor form basis of an action at law. Where conditions are essential, equity can enforce reconveyance. If assignor rescinds for breach of contract he must return purchase money/consideration already paid.

rubrics_metrics.name: Remedies when assignment procured by fraud of assignee
rubrics_metrics.description: If assignee obtained conveyance by fraud or unfair dealing, assignor may either treat conveyance as effective and recover damages equal to the value of the patent, or rescind the sale in equity on return of consideration and require the assignee to account for benefits received.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where assignee was not guilty of actual fraud but obtained patent for inadequate price through assignor's ignorance, the contract may be set aside upon repayment of purchase money plus reasonable compensation for assignee's services and expenses (cases cited).

rubrics_metrics.name: Assignor's action when assignee refuses to pay purchase money
rubrics_metrics.description: Upon neglect or refusal by the assignee to pay the purchase money, the assignor may recover the amount in assumpsit, debt, or covenant depending on contract form; various defenses may be urged against that action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Defenses available to assignee include defective title, invalidity of patent, fraud, or breach of warranty by assignor. Specific questions about these defenses have been much litigated and are elaborated in subsequent sections.

rubrics_metrics.name: Defective title as defense to action for purchase money
rubrics_metrics.description: An assignor whose title was defective at the time of conveyance, or who failed to confer a complete right, cannot claim the stipulated price; the assignee may withhold payment until title difficulties are removed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Defects include imperfect or unrecorded assignments, insufficient instruments to transfer legal title, or clouds on title. The burden of proof as to want of title lies on the assignee unless he has been actually disturbed in enjoyment of the invention. Unrecorded assignment generally gives vendor no title enabling suit for the price, subject to factual variations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patent invalidity as defense to recovery of purchase money
rubrics_metrics.description: An assignee may defend an action for the purchase money by showing that no patent corresponding to the assignment ever issued or that the patent is void (for want of novelty or utility, abandonment, defective specification, excessive claims, or substantial variations in a re-issue).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Invalidity is a defense on ground of failure of consideration. Courts distinguish lack of pecuniary market value (not a defense absent fraud/warranty) from lack of utility or patent-invalidating defects (which are defenses). Utility is presumed from existence of patent but can be disproved; if patent wholly void for want of utility, price cannot be recovered; if partially void as to some claims and apportionment possible, assignor can recover for valid portion. When assignee has used or profited from the patent, he should offer to return it and account for profits; if patent is void no actual return necessary. Evidence of invalidity may be collateral and certain procedural requirements (e.g., spreading equity on record) may be necessary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Market worthlessness vs. lack of patent utility
rubrics_metrics.description: Pecuniary worthlessness (market unsalability, being superseded) is not a defense to recovery of the purchase money in absence of fraud or warranty; but a want of utility in the invention itself (rendering patent void) is a good defense.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts draw a clear line: market failure does not equal lack of statutory utility. Uselessness sufficient to make the patent invalid (e.g., cannot be reduced to practice or will not answer intended purpose without further inventive skill) defeats recovery. Jury to judge of utility; utility is presumed from patent record until disproved.

rubrics_metrics.name: Requirement to offer return of patent and account when asserting defenses
rubrics_metrics.description: When assignee defends against an action for purchase money on grounds such as fraud or invalidity, he should offer to return the patent and account for benefits received; failure to do so may limit ability to rely on the defense.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where assignee used/derived benefits, he cannot simply retain benefits and avoid payment unless warranty/fraud exist; in defending he must return patent or tender reconveyance and render account or show he derived no benefits. When patent is found void, actual physical return may not be required.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fraudulent representations as defense (nature of representations)
rubrics_metrics.description: Fraudulent representations by the vendor that induced purchase are a defense to an action for the purchase money; such representations must be averments of existing facts (not mere opinions or puffing) and may relate to title, validity, or utility/value of the patented device.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assignee defending on fraud must offer to return the patent and show he derived no benefits or must render an account of benefits. Examples: representations that the invention was never before patented and never used except under the patent have been held to be good defenses to notes given for purchase. Fraud may also be proved by concealment of known defects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Breach of warranty as defense (implied and express)
rubrics_metrics.description: A breach of warranty (especially implied warranty of title or express warranty of validity) may constitute an entire or partial defense to an action for the purchase money, depending on the nature and effect of the broken covenant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Implied warranty of title and express warranty of validity are of the essence of the contract; breach relieves assignee from obligations. Other covenants judged by extent to which non-fulfillment impairs value; total failure of consideration defeats action, while partial/separable benefits may require apportioned payment. If price cannot be apportioned between advantage received and deprivation from breach, action fails.

rubrics_metrics.name: Waiver and contractual allocation concerning invalidity
rubrics_metrics.description: Parties may agree in the conveyance to provide for possible invalidity of the patent; such contractual provisions can waive or limit the assignee's right to defend on ground of invalidity or failure of consideration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If both parties provide in the conveyance for possible invalidity of patent, the vendee cannot in a suit for the price defend on the ground of want of consideration. Contract terms allocating risk/control preclude asserting invalidity contrary to agreed provisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prior-patent infringement defense and later patents
rubrics_metrics.description: That the patented invention infringes earlier patents has been declared a defense to recovery if the assignee was ignorant of that fact at time of purchase; the existence of a later patent for the same invention does not bar recovery by the assignor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evidence that a patent is void because it infringes a prior patent is not admissible in suit on a note given for a patent unless a competent federal court has declared it so. A later patent granted to another for same invention is no defense to a note for a prior patent.
